# Testing and Continuous Integration {#sec-testing} Your script reads a length-of-stay column from an institutional warehouse, and one quarter the warehouse begins reporting it in seconds where it previously reported days. Nothing errors. The column is still numeric, the join still succeeds, the model still fits, and every downstream number is wrong by a factor of 86,400. No amount of rereading your code will find the problem, because your code is not what changed. A one-line test asserting that length of stay falls in a plausible range fails on the first run after the change; this chapter is about writing that line, about finding out whether the tests you already have would notice anything at all, and about running them, through continuous integration, on a clean machine every time the code changes. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence.* [Edsger W. Dijkstra]{.smallcaps}, *Notes on Structured Programming* (1970) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: tests belong to the Analyze stage, beside the code they check, and continuous integration runs them again, with the rendered report, on a clean machine every time the code or the data change.](20-testing_files/figure-pdf/fig-testing-pipeline-1.pdf){#fig-testing-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Analyze.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 45 minutes. **You'll need.** @sec-wrangling for the `dplyr` verbs, @sec-types for dates and coded values, @sec-renv for the lockfile, @sec-quarto for rendering, and @sec-git-teams for pull requests. The code uses: ```r library(tinytest) library(palmerpenguins) ``` and calls `dplyr`, `tidyr`, and `janitor` with their namespaces. The CI chunks run R in fresh processes and need only `tinytest` and `knitr` installed. **You'll be able to.** - Write `tinytest` unit tests that assert values, boundaries, and errors, not only the shape of the output. - Build a small fixture that exercises every branch of a cleaning function, and pair it with an integration test on the real file. - Show that a test suite would catch a bug by planting one (mutation testing). - Read and write a GitHub Actions workflow that restores `renv.lock`, runs the tests with an exit status that fails the job, and renders the report. - Find the cause of a red run from the first error in its log, and fix it in the lockfile rather than in the workflow. - Harden a workflow: actions pinned by commit, a `permissions:` block, and no long-lived credentials. **Outline.** - [Why test an analysis](#sec-testing-why) - [Unit tests with tinytest](#sec-testing-unit) - [Structure versus correctness](#sec-testing-correctness) - [Test smells](#sec-testing-smells) - [Worked example: testing the HF-HOME CRF cleaner](#sec-testing-worked) - [Running tests in continuous integration](#sec-testing-ci) - [What CI proves](#sec-ci) - [Anatomy of a workflow](#sec-ci-anatomy) - [Reading a failing run](#sec-ci-reading) - [Securing the workflow](#sec-ci-security) - [For testthat readers](#sec-testing-testthat) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-20. 1. Why would you test a one-off data analysis script that will only ever run on a single dataset? 2. What is the difference between a unit test, an integration test, and an end-to-end test in the context of a data analysis pipeline? 3. What is continuous integration, and why is 'it renders on my machine' an insufficient guarantee that a collaborator can reproduce your analysis? ::: ## Why test an analysis {#sec-testing-why} Analysis code rarely gets tested, and the reason is a respectable one. Software is written to run on inputs its author has never seen; an analysis script is written to run on one dataset, once. The reasoning has two holes. The script does not run once: it runs every time an extract is refreshed, an exclusion is revised, or a reviewer asks for a sensitivity analysis, and by then its author has forgotten which branches were ever exercised. And the failures that matter in analysis code do not stop it running. A filter that removes the wrong rows, a join that duplicates a patient, a unit conversion applied twice: all produce output. The question a test answers is not 'did it run' but 'would I have noticed if it were wrong', and for most analysis scripts the honest answer is no. Three ordinary occasions make the case concrete (@tbl-testing-occasions). | Occasion | What changes | What the test asserts | |---|---|---| | Refactoring | Your code, on purpose: `base::merge()` becomes a `dplyr` join | The output is identical to a saved baseline | | Upstream drift | The data, silently: days become seconds | Values fall in plausible ranges; codes are in the codebook | | Documentation | Nobody's memory of the intent | Given input X, the function returns Y, and a false claim fails the build | : Three occasions a test pays for itself. {#tbl-testing-occasions} Tests come in layers that catch different failures (@fig-test-layers). For analysis code the pyramid familiar from software engineering is flatter: the integration layer, a small synthetic dataset run through the whole pipeline, does more work here than in most applications. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-test-layers %%| fig-alt: "Three stacked layers in increasing scope. Unit tests %%| exercise one function on known input, catch helper bugs, and %%| cost seconds. Integration tests run the whole pipeline on a %%| twenty-line synthetic dataset, catch composition bugs and %%| silent filter and join errors, and cost seconds. End-to-end %%| tests run raw data through to final figures, catch everything %%| remaining, and cost minutes to hours." %%| fig-cap: "The three test layers and what each one catches. %%| Unit tests are fast and narrow; end-to-end tests are slow and %%| broad; the integration layer, where a synthetic dataset is run %%| through the whole cleaning pipeline, has the best cost-benefit %%| ratio for analysis code and is the layer most often missing." flowchart TD U["Unit
one function, known input
catches: helper bugs
cost: seconds"] I["Integration
whole pipeline, 20-line
synthetic dataset
catches: composition bugs,
silent filter and join errors
cost: seconds"] E["End to end
raw data to final figures
catches: everything left
cost: minutes to hours"] U --> I --> E ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A cleaning script filters to adults with `filter(age >= 18)`. Six months later someone discovers that the export encodes unknown age as `-1`, so those rows were silently dropped as minors. Which layer would have caught it, and what would the test have asserted? **Answer.** The integration layer, and only if the synthetic dataset contained a `-1`. A unit test of the filter passes: given ages 17, 25, and 40 it correctly keeps two. The function is not broken; the *data* violated an assumption the function never stated. Two assertions are worth writing, and they fail at different times. One on the input, that `age` falls in a plausible range before the filter runs, fails the day the export changes. One on the output, that the number of rows dropped is what the codebook predicts, fails the day the meaning changes. The first is a claim about the data; the second is a claim about your understanding of it. ::: ## Unit tests with tinytest {#sec-testing-unit} The book uses `tinytest`. It has no dependencies of its own, which matters when the surrounding chapters are about pinning an environment; each test file runs on its own; and its assertion vocabulary is small enough to hold in your head. If you will work in a `testthat` project, @sec-testing-testthat translates. For a function in `R/clean.R`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} #' Compute age groups from numeric age #' @param age numeric vector age_group <- function(age) { cut(age, breaks = c(0, 18, 40, 65, Inf), right = FALSE, labels = c("under-18", "18-39", "40-64", "65+")) } ``` ::: Tests in `inst/tinytest/test-clean.R`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tinytest) expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(20, 50, 75))), c("18-39", "40-64", "65+"), info = "typical adult ages bin correctly") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(20, 50, 75))), c("18-39", #> call| "40-64", "65+"), info = "typical adult ages bin correctly") #> info| typical adult ages bin correctly # the interval starts are inclusive, because right = FALSE expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(18, 40, 65))), c("18-39", "40-64", "65+"), info = "boundary values fall in the upper bin") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(18, 40, 65))), c("18-39", #> call| "40-64", "65+"), info = "boundary values fall in the upper bin") #> info| boundary values fall in the upper bin expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(17, 39, 64))), c("under-18", "18-39", "40-64"), info = "values just below a break stay below") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(as.character(age_group(c(17, 39, 64))), c("under-18", #> call| "18-39", "40-64"), info = "values just below a break stay below") #> info| values just below a break stay below # NA_real_, not NA: bare NA is logical, and cut() rejects it. The # distinction is invisible until the test is actually run. expect_true(is.na(age_group(NA_real_)), info = "numeric NA propagates rather than erroring") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_true(is.na(age_group(NA)), info = "numeric NA propagates rather than erroring") #> info| numeric NA propagates rather than erroring expect_error(age_group("twenty"), info = "non-numeric input is rejected") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_error(age_group("twenty"), info = "non-numeric input is rejected") #> info| non-numeric input is rejected ``` ::: Each `expect_*()` call is one test, and its `info=` string says what it checks; a failure reports the file and line beside it. The tests above follow the rule that edge cases are where bugs live: boundaries, missing values, and the wrong type. For other functions the list includes empty input, a single observation, a group with one member, zero variance, and perfect collinearity. Run every test file from the project root, or a package's tests by name (display-only; both need a project with an `inst/tinytest/` directory): ```r tinytest::test_all() tinytest::test_package("practicum") ``` `tinytest` expects the test files in `inst/tinytest/` and a one-line `tests/tinytest.R` that runs them, which is the layout `tinytest::setup_tinytest()` creates and the one `zzcollab` scaffolds. Tests under `inst/` are installed with the package, so someone who has your compendium can run its tests without your source tree. For an analysis whose credibility rests on being checkable by someone else, that is the right default. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Written as `expect_true(is.na(age_group(NA)))`, the `NA` test errors instead of passing. What does that tell you about the function, beyond the test? **Answer.** Bare `NA` is logical, and `cut()` requires a numeric argument, so `age_group(NA)` stops with `'x' must be numeric`. The same input arises in production: a column that is empty in every row is read by `read.csv()` as logical, and the function then fails on it. The test has found a real input the function does not handle, which is what a test is for. ::: ### Exercises 1. `age_group()` is tested for typical ages, boundaries, `NA`, and non-numeric input. One gap remains: what the function does with an age outside the range the breaks cover. Find the behavior, decide whether it is the behavior you want, and write the test that pins whichever answer you choose. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} as.character(age_group(c(-5, 0, 200))) #> [1] NA "under-18" "65+" ``` ::: A negative age returns `NA`, because the breaks begin at 0 and `cut()` places anything below the first break outside every interval. An age of 200 is absorbed into `65+`, because the last break is `Inf`. The asymmetry is the finding: an impossible age at the top of the range is silently accepted, and an impossible age at the bottom becomes the same `NA` a genuinely missing age produces. Pinning the current behavior: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} expect_true(is.na(age_group(-5)), info = "age below the first break gives NA") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_true(is.na(age_group(-5)), info = "age below the first break gives NA") #> info| age below the first break gives NA ``` ::: Preferring an error instead, the test comes first and the function changes to satisfy it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} age_group_strict <- function(age) { stopifnot(is.numeric(age)) if (any(age < 0, na.rm = TRUE)) stop("negative age") cut(age, breaks = c(0, 18, 40, 65, Inf), right = FALSE, labels = c("under-18", "18-39", "40-64", "65+")) } expect_error(age_group_strict(-5), pattern = "negative age", info = "negative age is rejected") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_error(age_group_strict(-5), pattern = "negative age", #> call| info = "negative age is rejected") #> info| negative age is rejected expect_equal(as.character(age_group_strict(30)), "18-39", info = "a valid age still bins correctly") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(as.character(age_group_strict(30)), "18-39", info = "a valid age still bins correctly") #> info| a valid age still bins correctly ``` ::: Either is defensible. Leaving the behavior untested is not, because then it is not a decision at all, only whatever `cut()` happened to do. ::: ## Structure versus correctness {#sec-testing-correctness} A test that the result 'is a tibble of the right shape' is a structural check, not a test of correctness. A test that a regression coefficient on a known synthetic dataset equals the closed-form answer, or that a cell survives the pipeline unchanged, is a test of correctness. Write both, and do not mistake the first for the second. ### Integration tests on synthetic data Unit tests catch helper bugs. They do not catch bugs where the helpers work individually and their composition fails. An integration test runs the whole pipeline on a small synthetic dataset: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # inst/tinytest/test-pipeline.R # In a package the test file would load run_pipeline from R/; it is # defined here so the example executes as written. run_pipeline <- function(raw) { raw |> janitor::clean_names() |> dplyr::filter(age >= 18) |> dplyr::mutate(age_group = age_group(age)) |> tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::starts_with("bp_"), names_to = "visit", names_prefix = "bp_v", values_to = "bp") |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(bp)) |> dplyr::mutate(visit = as.integer(visit)) |> dplyr::select(patient_id, age_group, sex, treatment, visit, bp) } # synthetic data that exercises every branch raw <- tibble::tibble( patient_id = c(1, 2, 3, 4), age = c(25, 50, 75, 17), # one excluded bp_v1 = c(120, 140, 160, NA), bp_v2 = c(118, 138, NA, NA), sex = c("M", "F", "F", "M"), treatment = c("placebo", "active", "placebo", "active") ) clean <- run_pipeline(raw) expect_inherits(clean, "tbl_df", info = "returns a tibble") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_inherits(clean, "tbl_df", info = "returns a tibble") #> info| returns a tibble expect_equal(names(clean), c("patient_id", "age_group", "sex", "treatment", "visit", "bp"), info = "column names and order are as specified") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(names(clean), c("patient_id", "age_group", "sex", #> call| "treatment", "visit", "bp"), info = "column names and order are as specified") #> info| column names and order are as specified # row count: 3 adults x 2 visits, minus NAs expect_equal(nrow(clean), 5, info = "patient 4 excluded; patient 3 has one NA bp") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(nrow(clean), 5, info = "patient 4 excluded; patient 3 has one NA bp") #> info| patient 4 excluded; patient 3 has one NA bp expect_equal(clean$bp[clean$patient_id == 1 & clean$visit == 1], 120, info = "a known cell survives the pipeline unchanged") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(clean$bp[clean$patient_id == 1 & clean$visit == #> call| 1], 120, info = "a known cell survives the pipeline unchanged") #> info| a known cell survives the pipeline unchanged ``` ::: The dataset has four patients and two visits, but it exercises each cleaning rule: the age exclusion (patient 4) and a missing value (patient 3, visit 2). The rule generalizes: for each filter, derivation, pivot, and recode, the fixture has at least one row that exercises it, including the branches you do not think exist. ### Reference tests For an output that is tedious to assert literally, compare it with a stored reference. The first run writes the object to a file and passes; later runs compare against it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ref_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "lm-coefs.rds") unlink(ref_file) fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars) refit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars[-1, ]) c(first_run = expect_equal_to_reference(coef(fit), ref_file), later_run = expect_equal_to_reference(coef(fit), ref_file), changed = expect_equal_to_reference(coef(refit), ref_file)) #> first_run later_run changed #> TRUE TRUE FALSE ``` ::: When a reference test fails, you decide whether the change is intended (delete the file and regenerate it) or a regression. The stored object is compared by value, so a coefficient that changed fails and a `print` method that gained a blank line does not. Inspect the reference once when it is first written, because the first run accepts whatever the code produced. | Use a reference test when | Avoid it when | |---|---| | The output is complex and tedious to assert literally | The output changes for trivial reasons: an unseeded random draw, the locale, an unstable sort | | The question is 'is this what was reviewed' | The stored object is too large to inspect when it changes, so 'accept or investigate' becomes a coin toss | : When a reference test helps. {#tbl-testing-reference} ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Your test asserts `expect_equal(nrow(result), 100)`, and it passes. Does this mean the result is correct? **Answer.** No. It says nothing about which rows, what values, or whether the right rows were filtered; 100 rows of the wrong patients pass. Add assertions on content: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} result <- data.frame(patient_id = 1:100, age = rep(40:49, 10)) expected_ids <- 1:100 expected_ages <- rep(40:49, 10) expect_equal(nrow(result), 100) # structural #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(nrow(result), 100) expect_equal(sort(result$patient_id), # correctness sort(expected_ids)) #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(sort(result$patient_id), sort(expected_ids)) expect_equal(result$age, expected_ages) #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(result$age, expected_ages) ``` ::: 'Looks right at the surface, wrong underneath' is the most common testing failure in data analysis, and a structural test alone is built to miss it. ::: ### Exercises 2. Write a `summarize_species()` function returning mean body mass and count per species from `palmerpenguins::penguins`. Give it one structural test and one correctness test, and say in a comment which is which and why the structural one is insufficient on its own. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(palmerpenguins) summarize_species <- function(data) { data |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |> dplyr::group_by(species) |> dplyr::summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") } # STRUCTURAL: shape only. Every line below passes even if # mean_mass is computed as a median, a sum, or the wrong column. out <- summarize_species(penguins) expect_inherits(out, "tbl_df", info = "structural: a tibble") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_inherits(out, "tbl_df", info = "structural: a tibble") #> info| structural: a tibble expect_equal(names(out), c("species", "mean_mass", "n"), info = "structural: column names") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(names(out), c("species", "mean_mass", "n"), info = "structural: column names") #> info| structural: column names expect_equal(nrow(out), 3, info = "structural: one row per species") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(nrow(out), 3, info = "structural: one row per species") #> info| structural: one row per species # CORRECTNESS: values the test computes independently. adelie <- penguins$body_mass_g[penguins$species == "Adelie"] expect_equal(out$mean_mass[out$species == "Adelie"], mean(adelie, na.rm = TRUE), info = "correctness: the mean is the mean") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(out$mean_mass[out$species == "Adelie"], mean(adelie, #> call| na.rm = TRUE), info = "correctness: the mean is the mean") #> info| correctness: the mean is the mean expect_equal(out$n[out$species == "Adelie"], sum(!is.na(adelie)), info = "correctness: n counts non-missing") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(out$n[out$species == "Adelie"], sum(!is.na(adelie)), #> call| info = "correctness: n counts non-missing") #> info| correctness: n counts non-missing ``` ::: The structural test is worth keeping, because a change in column names breaks callers. It is insufficient because every assertion in it would still pass if `mean()` were replaced by `median()`. Only the second test would fail, and only because it recomputes the answer a different way rather than comparing the function with itself. ::: ## Test smells {#sec-testing-smells} Some tests look like tests and produce only confidence. Two run below; @tbl-testing-smells lists the common kinds. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # foo ignores its argument and always returns 42. It is wrong for # every input, and the test below still passes. foo <- function(x) 42 expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1), # always passes info = "foo works") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1), info = "foo works") #> info| foo works ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} result <- 0.9 # nowhere near 0.5 expect_equal(result, 0.5, tolerance = 0.5) # passes for 0 to 1 #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(result, 0.5, tolerance = 0.5) ``` ::: The tolerance example passes for any value from 0 to 1. With an expected value no larger than the tolerance, `all.equal()`, which `expect_equal()` uses, compares the absolute difference, so a tolerance of 0.5 around 0.5 accepts every proportion there is. | Smell | Example | Why it misleads | Fix | |---|---|---|---| | Tautology | `expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1))` | Compares the function with itself | Compare with a value computed another way | | Mocking the code under test | A stub `fit_model <- function(d) list()` inside the test | Tests the stub, not the function | Test the real function on a small input | | Brittle reference | `expect_equal_to_reference(do_thing(Sys.Date()), ...)` | Fails every day after the first, so failures stop being read | Remove the date, or compare stable fields | | Permissive tolerance | `expect_equal(x, 0.5, tolerance = 0.5)` | Accepts any proportion | Set the tolerance from the computation's real precision | | Placeholder | `expect_true(TRUE)` | Tests nothing | Write the test or delete the line | | Prefixed expectation | `tinytest::expect_equal(x, y)` in a test file | Not collected: the file reports zero tests, with only a message | Call `expect_equal()` without the prefix | | Shape only | `expect_equal(nrow(out), 100)` | Passes on the wrong rows | Assert values (@sec-testing-correctness) | : Test smells. Watch for them in code review. {#tbl-testing-smells} `tinytest` has no mocking facility, which makes the second smell harder to write by accident than under `testthat`'s `with_mocked_bindings()`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A colleague's test is `expect_equal(risk_difference(d), risk_difference(d), tolerance = 1e-8)`. They point out that the tolerance is tight. Is the test any good? **Answer.** No. It is a tautology with a tight tolerance: the expected value comes from calling the function under test, so it passes whatever the function returns. The tolerance is irrelevant. The fix is an expected value computed another way, for example the difference of two proportions worked out by hand on a ten-row fixture. ::: ### Exercises 3. Replace the tautological test, `expect_equal(foo(1), foo(1))`, with an assertion that fails against `foo <- function(x) 42` while passing against a correct implementation that doubles its argument. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} foo <- function(x) 42 # wrong for every input expect_equal(foo(1), 2, info = "foo doubles 1") #> ----- FAILED[data]: <--> #> call| expect_equal(foo(1), 2, info = "foo doubles 1") #> diff| Expected '2', got '42' #> info| foo doubles 1 expect_equal(foo(3), 6, info = "foo doubles 3") #> ----- FAILED[data]: <--> #> call| expect_equal(foo(3), 6, info = "foo doubles 3") #> diff| Expected '6', got '42' #> info| foo doubles 3 ``` ::: The fix is to assert against a value computed independently of the function, here by hand. Any assertion whose expected value comes from calling the function is circular, and no number of added cases repairs that. ::: ## Worked example: testing the HF-HOME CRF cleaner {#sec-testing-worked} The HF-HOME CRF (case report form) export, `analysis/data/raw_data/hfhome/crf_export.csv`, comes from five site systems that each write the same fields differently: Site D codes sex as `1` and `2`, Site C writes dates month first, Site E has lost the leading zeros of its patient IDs, and the site labels vary in case and spacing. The function below puts four fields into canonical form. Each site's coding lives in a lookup table passed as an argument with a default, so that the codebook is in one place and a change to it is a one-line change. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} #' Clean the site-specific fields of the HF-HOME CRF export #' #' @param raw Data frame read from `crf_export.csv`, every column #' character. #' @param site_d_sex Codes Site D uses for sex. #' @param date_formats Discharge-date format for each site. #' @return A data frame of `patient_id`, `site`, `sex`, and #' `discharge_date` in canonical form. clean_crf <- function(raw, site_d_sex = c("1" = "M", "2" = "F"), date_formats = c("Site A" = "%Y-%m-%d", "Site B" = "%Y-%m-%d", "Site C" = "%m/%d/%Y", "Site D" = "%d-%b-%Y", "Site E" = "%Y%m%d")) { site <- paste("Site", toupper(substring(trimws(raw$site), 6))) sex <- ifelse(site == "Site D", site_d_sex[raw$sex], toupper(substr(raw$sex, 1, 1))) if (!all(sex %in% c("F", "M"))) { stop("unrecognized sex code: ", paste(unique(raw$sex[!sex %in% c("F", "M")]), collapse = ", ")) } data.frame( patient_id = sprintf("%04d", as.integer(raw$patient_id)), site = site, sex = unname(sex), discharge_date = as.Date(raw$discharge_date, format = date_formats[site]) ) } ``` ::: The test file has two layers. The unit layer is a fixture with one row per site, each written the way that site writes it, and expected values worked out by hand from the codebook. The integration layer cleans the whole export and compares it with two independent records of the same patients: sex in the registration demographics and the discharge date in the baseline table. Agreement between independent sources is a check real trials run, and it needs no hand-written expectations.[^locale] [^locale]: `%b` matches English month abbreviations only in an English locale. On a machine whose `LC_TIME` is set otherwise, Site D's dates parse to `NA`, and the date tests below report it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # inst/tinytest/test-clean-crf.R hf_dir <- Sys.getenv("HFHOME_DIR") fixture <- data.frame( patient_id = c("0005", "0001", "0012", "0010", "7"), site = c("Site A", "site b", "SITE C", " Site D", "Site E "), sex = c("F", "Male", "f", "2", "M"), discharge_date = c("2024-02-02", "2024-02-01", "02/03/2024", "05-FEB-2024", "20240209") ) out <- clean_crf(fixture) expect_equal(out$patient_id, c("0005", "0001", "0012", "0010", "0007"), info = "Site E IDs regain their leading zeros") expect_equal(out$site, paste("Site", LETTERS[1:5]), info = "site labels are normalized") expect_equal(out$sex, c("F", "M", "F", "F", "M"), info = "every site's sex coding; Site D codes 2 as F") expect_equal(out$discharge_date, as.Date(c("2024-02-02", "2024-02-01", "2024-02-03", "2024-02-05", "2024-02-09")), info = "every site's date format; Site C is month first") expect_error(clean_crf(transform(fixture, sex = "X")), pattern = "unrecognized sex code", info = "an unknown sex code stops the cleaning") crf <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"), colClasses = "character", fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM") demographics <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "demographics.csv"), colClasses = "character") baseline <- read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "baseline.csv"), colClasses = "character") both <- merge(clean_crf(crf), demographics[c("patient_id", "sex")], by = "patient_id", suffixes = c("", "_demo")) both <- merge(both, baseline[c("patient_id", "discharge_date")], by = "patient_id", suffixes = c("", "_base")) expect_equal(nrow(both), nrow(crf), info = "every CRF patient is found in both sources") expect_equal(both$sex, both$sex_demo, info = "sex agrees with the registration record") expect_equal(both$discharge_date, as.Date(both$discharge_date_base), info = "discharge date agrees with the baseline table") ``` ::: In a project this chunk is the file `inst/tinytest/test-clean-crf.R`. The chunk below writes it to a temporary file and runs it as `tinytest` would, with the data directory passed in an environment variable rather than written into the test. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} test_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "test-clean-crf.R") writeLines(knitr::knit_code$get("test-crf-tests"), test_file) hf_env <- list( HFHOME_DIR = normalizePath(file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")) ) passing <- run_test_file(test_file, verbose = 0, set_env = hf_env) passing #> All ok, 8 results (48ms) ``` ::: Every test passes. That shows the tests agree with the function; it does not yet show that they would notice if the function were wrong. To find out, plant a bug a reviewer could plausibly miss, here Site D's sex codes swapped, and run the same tests again: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} clean_crf_correct <- clean_crf clean_crf <- function(raw) { clean_crf_correct(raw, site_d_sex = c("1" = "F", "2" = "M")) } mutant <- run_test_file(test_file, verbose = 0, set_env = hf_env) mutant #> ----- FAILED[data]: test-clean-crf.R<17--18> #> call| expect_equal(out$sex, c("F", "M", "F", "F", "M"), info = "every site's sex coding; Site D codes 2 as F") #> diff| 1 string mismatch #> info| every site's sex coding; Site D codes 2 as F #> ----- FAILED[data]: test-clean-crf.R<40--41> #> call| expect_equal(both$sex, both$sex_demo, info = "sex agrees with the registration record") #> diff| 373 string mismatches #> info| sex agrees with the registration record #> #> Showing 2 out of 8 results: 2 fails, 6 passes (43ms) clean_crf <- clean_crf_correct ``` ::: Both layers catch it: the fixture's Site D row, and the comparison with the registration record, which disagrees for every Site D patient. The swapped function returns a plausible data frame, with two sexes in plausible proportions, which is exactly the kind of bug that survives inspection (Habit 8). This check has a name: **mutation testing** [@demillo1978hints]. Each planted bug is a *mutant*; a test that fails on it *kills* it; and the share of mutants killed measures how much the suite can see. Tools for other languages generate mutants automatically (flipped comparisons, swapped constants, deleted lines). By hand, plant one mutant per rule in the codebook, starting with the rules whose failure would produce a plausible number. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Confirm in code that the suite passes the correct function and fails the mutant, so that a later edit to the tests cannot quietly make them blind to it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot(tinytest::all_pass(passing), tinytest::any_fail(mutant)) ``` ::: The chunk prints nothing when both hold. ::: ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} An agentic version: a coding agent writes tests and runs mutants, and you review the evidence rather than only the code. > **Context.** `R/clean_crf.R` cleans the HF-HOME CRF export. The > codebook, `analysis/data/raw_data/hfhome/README.md`, lists each > site's coding of sex, dates, IDs, and site labels. Existing tests > are in `inst/tinytest/`. Run code only against the synthetic > HF-HOME files. > > **Constraints.** Add tests in a new file, > `inst/tinytest/test-clean-crf-sites.R`. Do not edit > `R/clean_crf.R` or any existing test file, do not skip, delete, > or loosen a test, and add no packages. If a test you write fails > against the current function, stop and report it; do not change > the test to make it pass. > > **Criteria.** Before writing tests, list each codebook rule and > the fixture row that will exercise it. Then, for each rule, > create one mutant of `clean_crf()` in a temporary copy, run the > suite against it, and report a table of mutant, killed or > survived, and the test that killed it. *Failure mode.* An agent told to make tests pass will weaken them: it widens a tolerance, replaces a value check with a shape check, or edits the expected value to match the output. That is why the instruction forbids touching existing tests, and why the rule that tests are off-limits to an agent is part of the book's governance rules (@sec-ai-governance). *Check.* Run `git diff --stat -- inst/tinytest/ R/` and confirm that only the new test file changed; read every `expect_*()` in it for a hand-derived expected value; then run one mutant yourself, as in the chunk above, and confirm that the suite fails. The codebook and synthetic files hold no patient data. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Why does the fixture have one row per site, written by hand, rather than five rows sampled from the export? **Answer.** Every pathology in the export is per site, so a test must exercise every site to exercise every branch. Five sampled rows can easily miss Site D, whose numeric sex codes are the branch most likely to be wrong, and a sample changes when the export does. A hand-built row per site exercises each branch on purpose, and its expected values come from the codebook rather than from the function. ::: ### Exercises 4. Make a second mutant that parses Site C's dates day first (`"%d/%m/%Y"`). Predict which tests kill it, run the suite, and count how many Site C dates the mutant gets silently wrong, rather than `NA`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} day_first <- eval(formals(clean_crf_correct)$date_formats) day_first["Site C"] <- "%d/%m/%Y" clean_crf <- function(raw) { clean_crf_correct(raw, date_formats = day_first) } mutant_c <- run_test_file(test_file, verbose = 0, set_env = hf_env) mutant_c #> ----- FAILED[data]: test-clean-crf.R<19--22> #> call| expect_equal(out$discharge_date, as.Date(c("2024-02-02", "2024-02-01", #> call| --> "2024-02-03", "2024-02-05", "2024-02-09")), info = "every site's date format; Site C is month first") #> diff| Mean relative difference: 0.001417291 #> info| every site's date format; Site C is month first #> ----- FAILED[data]: test-clean-crf.R<42--43> #> call| expect_equal(both$discharge_date, as.Date(both$discharge_date_base), #> call| --> info = "discharge date agrees with the baseline table") #> diff| 'is.NA' value mismatch: 271 in current 0 in target #> info| discharge date agrees with the baseline table #> #> Showing 2 out of 8 results: 2 fails, 6 passes (38ms) crf <- read.csv(file.path(hf_env$HFHOME_DIR, "crf_export.csv"), colClasses = "character", fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM") right <- clean_crf_correct(crf) wrong <- clean_crf(crf) in_c <- right$site == "Site C" c(site_c = sum(in_c), became_na = sum(is.na(wrong$discharge_date[in_c])), silently_wrong = sum(!is.na(wrong$discharge_date[in_c]) & wrong$discharge_date[in_c] != right$discharge_date[in_c])) #> site_c became_na silently_wrong #> 498 271 207 clean_crf <- clean_crf_correct ``` ::: The fixture's date test and the comparison with the baseline table both kill the mutant. The counts show why the comparison matters more than it seems: dates whose day is above 12 become `NA`, which is loud, but every date whose day is 12 or below, and differs from its month, parses to a valid date in the wrong month. The third count is the one that matters: those dates pass every check except a comparison with something independent. ::: 5. The CRF's `sbp_discharge` column marks a missing value three ways: an empty field, `NA`, and `-99`. Write `clean_sbp()`, which returns numeric systolic blood pressure with every missing code as `NA`, and a test that compares it with `sbp_discharge` in `baseline.csv`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} clean_sbp <- function(x) { x <- trimws(x) x[x %in% c("", "NA", "-99")] <- NA as.numeric(x) } crf_raw <- read.csv(file.path(hf_env$HFHOME_DIR, "crf_export.csv"), colClasses = "character", fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM", na.strings = character()) crf_raw$patient_id <- sprintf("%04d", as.integer(crf_raw$patient_id)) baseline <- read.csv(file.path(hf_env$HFHOME_DIR, "baseline.csv"), colClasses = c(patient_id = "character")) both <- merge(crf_raw[c("patient_id", "sbp_discharge")], baseline[c("patient_id", "sbp_discharge")], by = "patient_id", suffixes = c("_crf", "_base")) expect_equal(clean_sbp(both$sbp_discharge_crf), as.numeric(both$sbp_discharge_base), info = "every missing code becomes NA; values unchanged") #> ----- PASSED : <--> #> call| expect_equal(clean_sbp(both$sbp_discharge_crf), as.numeric(both$sbp_discharge_base), #> call| info = "every missing code becomes NA; values unchanged") #> info| every missing code becomes NA; values unchanged c(missing_crf = sum(is.na(clean_sbp(both$sbp_discharge_crf))), missing_baseline = sum(is.na(both$sbp_discharge_base))) #> missing_crf missing_baseline #> 78 78 ``` ::: `na.strings = character()` keeps the raw codes as text, so that the function, not `read.csv()`, decides what is missing; with the default, `NA` is converted on reading and `-99` is not, and the test would no longer exercise the function's handling of either. A version that forgot `-99` would leave impossible pressures of -99 mmHg in the data, which a mean would absorb without complaint; the comparison with the baseline table fails on it. ::: ## Running tests in continuous integration {#sec-testing-ci} Tests that run only when someone remembers to run them catch regressions late. Continuous integration (CI) runs them on every push. This section sets up the minimal workflow and shows why its exit status matters; the four sections that follow, from @sec-ci, cover what a green check proves, how a workflow is built, how to read a red run, and how to secure the workflow. For an R package, `usethis::use_github_action("check-standard")` sets up GitHub Actions to run `R CMD check`, which runs the tests, on several operating systems and R versions. For an analysis project, the equivalent is a workflow that runs the tests. It assumes a `DESCRIPTION` file listing the project's dependencies, as a research compendium has; without one, replace `local::.` with the packages the tests need: ```yaml # .github/workflows/test.yaml name: tests on: [push, pull_request] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2 - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2 with: packages: | local::. any::tinytest - name: Run tests run: | Rscript -e 'res <- tinytest::test_all()' \ -e 'quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))' ``` ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **A green CI job can contain failing tests.** The second `-e` line is not optional. `tinytest::test_all()` reports failures but returns normally, so `Rscript` exits with status 0 and the job stays green however many tests fail. A CI step fails only on a nonzero exit status, so the script must turn 'any test failed' into one. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Run a one-test suite that fails, in a fresh R process as CI would, with and without the `quit()` line, and compare the exit statuses. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} failing <- file.path(tempdir(), "failing-suite") dir.create(failing, showWarnings = FALSE) writeLines("expect_equal(1 + 1, 3)", file.path(failing, "test-fail.R")) r_libs <- paste0("R_LIBS=", paste(.libPaths(), collapse = .Platform$path.sep)) rscript <- function(...) { system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript"), shQuote(c("--vanilla", ...)), env = r_libs, stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE) } run_suite <- sprintf("res <- tinytest::run_test_dir('%s')", failing) c(without_quit = rscript("-e", run_suite), with_quit = rscript("-e", run_suite, "-e", "quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))")) #> without_quit with_quit #> 0 1 ``` ::: Status 0 is what CI reads as success. Only the version with `quit()` reports the failing test as a failure. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A teammate's workflow runs `Rscript -e 'tinytest::test_all()'` and has been green for a month. What do you know about the tests? **Answer.** Only that the R process started and `test_all()` returned. Without the `quit(status = ...)` line, a run in which every test failed also exits with status 0. Open the log of the latest run and read the summary line, then add the `quit()` line and push a deliberately failing test to see the job turn red. ::: ## What CI proves {#sec-ci} You install `janitor` in March to clean column names, the analysis renders on your laptop, and you never run `renv::snapshot()`. In June you open a pull request, and a red cross appears beside it. The log ends with `Error: Process completed with exit code 1.`, which tells you nothing; a dozen lines above it is the line that tells you everything, `there is no package called 'janitor'`. Your laptop remembered the package and the lockfile did not, so without the red cross a collaborator would have found out at submission. Continuous integration runs the analysis on a machine that is not yours, from a clean state, on every push; this section and the three after it are about making it check what matters and reading what it reports. Continuous integration (CI) is the practice of building and checking a project automatically every time it changes. When you push a commit, a fresh machine in the cloud checks out the code, reconstructs the environment, runs the tests, and renders the report; if anything fails, you are told within minutes. This chapter uses GitHub Actions, the CI system built into GitHub, because it is free for public repositories and the R community maintains ready-made steps for it. Triggers, jobs, and steps on a clean machine transfer unchanged to GitLab CI and the other systems. For a statistician the value is specific. A passing test suite says the code does what its tests check. A passing CI run says more: that the analysis reconstructs from `renv.lock` on a machine that is not yours and produces the report. That second guarantee is the one that matters when a reviewer, or you in a year, must rerun the work. The workflow file is boilerplate and can be copied; what it checks, and therefore what a green check entitles you to claim, is a decision. ### What a green check is worth A green check is only as good as what the workflow runs. @tbl-ci-checklist lists the four things a workflow for an analysis compendium should establish, in the order the steps run. | Check | Step | What a pass proves | What it does not prove | |---|---|---|---| | The environment restores | `setup-renv` (`renv::restore()`) | Every package in `renv.lock` installs on a clean machine | That the lockfile lists every package the code uses | | The tests pass | `tinytest`, with an exit status | The statistical checks of @sec-testing-correctness and @sec-testing-worked hold on known inputs | Anything the tests do not assert | | The report renders | `quarto render` | Every chunk runs from committed files, with no manual step | That the numbers in it are right | | No secrets in the repository | Review, and the platform's encrypted secrets | Credentials live outside version control | That printed values are masked; see @sec-ci-security | : The CI checklist for an analysis compendium. A workflow that restores and renders but does not test proves that the report compiles, not that it is correct. {#tbl-ci-checklist} The first row has a gap that the `janitor` story falls into. A restore installs what the lockfile lists, so a package the lockfile omits does not fail the restore; it fails the first later step that loads it. That is why the rows are a stack, not a menu: the test and render steps are what discover that the restore was incomplete. Fail loudly and early. Humble and Farley's advice for software delivery, 'if it hurts, do it more frequently, and bring the pain forward' [@humble2010continuous], applies unchanged to research code. The purpose of CI is to surface a break at the commit that introduced it, when the cause is one small diff, rather than at submission, when the cause is buried in months of history. Every step must fail the job when its check fails, not warn and continue. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Your workflow restores `renv` and renders the report, and the check is green. A collaborator reports that a figure differs from yours. What does the green check tell you, and what does it not? **Answer.** It tells you that the analysis reconstructs from `renv.lock` on a clean machine and that the report renders, so the discrepancy is not a missing package or an uncommitted file. It does not tell you the figure is correct, because nothing in the workflow tests the figure's content. Suspect an unseeded random step, a different data version, or a genuine analytic difference, and add a test that pins the figure's underlying numbers so that CI catches the change next time. ::: ### Exercises 6. A workflow restores `renv.lock`, runs a `tinytest` suite whose only test checks that the analytic dataset has the expected columns, and renders the report. For each change below, say which step turns the run red, or whether the run stays green. (a) The code calls `janitor`, which is installed on your laptop but absent from the lockfile. (b) A chunk reads `data/derived/cohort.rds`, a file listed in `.gitignore`. (c) The primary analysis computes a median where the plan specifies a mean. (d) Someone pastes an API token into the workflow file. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} (a) Not the restore, which succeeds because it installs only what the lockfile lists; the run turns red at the first step that loads `janitor`, the tests if they call it, otherwise the render. (b) The render: the file exists on your machine and not on the runner. (c) Nothing; the run stays green, because the only test checks the shape of the data, not a value (Habit 9). (d) Nothing; the run stays green, and the token is now in the Git history of a repository that may be public. Revoke it, then move it to the platform's encrypted secrets. Two of the four failures pass every step, which is the point of the last column of @tbl-ci-checklist. ::: ## Anatomy of a workflow {#sec-ci-anatomy} A GitHub Actions workflow is a YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) file in `.github/workflows/`. It names the events that trigger it, one or more jobs, and the steps within each job. The steps run in order on a fresh virtual machine, called a runner, that GitHub provisions for the run. @fig-ci-anatomy is the shape before the syntax. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-ci-anatomy %%| fig-alt: "Flowchart of a CI workflow run. The `on` block runs the workflow on every push to `main` and on every pull request. The single job, `check`, runs on a fresh Ubuntu runner. Its steps check out the code, install R, restore the exact package versions in `renv.lock`, install Quarto, run the test suite, and render the report. If any step exits with a nonzero status, the job fails and GitHub marks the commit with a red cross; if every step exits zero, a green check. ### Three details that decide the result **The runner has only what the workflow installs.** R is there because `setup-r` installed it and Quarto because `quarto-actions/setup` did; drop the Quarto step and the render fails with 'command not found'. **The test step must fail on a failed test.** The second `-e` expression turns 'any test failed' into a nonzero exit status, which is the only signal CI reads; without it the job stays green however many tests fail, as the demonstration in @sec-testing-ci showed. **Restore the lockfile, not the latest versions.** The `r-lib/actions` collection supplies two ways to provide packages, and they are alternatives, not companions: | Step | Installs | CI then tests | |---|---|---| | `setup-renv` | The exact versions recorded in `renv.lock` | The environment you pinned | | `setup-r-dependencies` | Current versions of the packages a `DESCRIPTION` file names | Whatever CRAN offers today | The minimal workflow of @sec-testing-ci uses `setup-r-dependencies`, which suits a package that must work with current versions. A compendium with a lockfile wants `setup-renv`, and every package the tests call, `tinytest` included, must therefore be in the lockfile. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **`continue-on-error: true` turns a red step green.** The setting is sometimes added to a test step 'until the tests are fixed'. The step still fails, but the job is reported as passing, so the commit gets a green check, branch protection lets the pull request merge, and nobody opens the log. Remove the setting and fix or delete the failing test instead. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Before you push, run the two R steps the way CI will, in a fresh process from the project root (display-only): ```bash Rscript -e 'renv::status()' Rscript -e 'res <- tinytest::test_all()' \ -e 'quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))' echo $? ``` `renv::status()` should report no issues, and the last line should print 0. With a failing test planted, it should print 1, as in @sec-testing-ci. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A teammate replaces `setup-renv` with `setup-r-dependencies` because the restore 'kept failing', and the run turns green. What has the green check stopped proving? **Answer.** That the analysis reproduces with the package versions in `renv.lock`. The run now tests whatever versions CRAN serves today, so a result that changed because a dependency changed would pass without notice, which is the silent regression @sec-renv exists to prevent. Find out why the restore failed (usually a system library, @sec-ci-reading) and fix that instead. ::: ### Exercises 7. Add a weekly scheduled run, at 06:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) every Monday, to the workflow above, and explain what a scheduled run catches in a project whose packages are pinned. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} Add a `schedule` trigger to the `on` block: ```yaml on: push: branches: [main] pull_request: schedule: - cron: '0 6 * * 1' ``` The five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week (1 is Monday), in UTC. A pinned lockfile does not mean nothing changes: the runner image is updated, archived package sources move, and an external data source or URL the report reads can disappear. A weekly run finds these on a quiet Monday rather than on the day you need to rerun the analysis. ::: ## Reading a failing run {#sec-ci-reading} When a run fails, GitHub shows the job's log with the failing step expanded. Read it from the first error, not from the bottom: the first error is usually the cause, and everything below it is consequence. The chunk below reproduces the `janitor` story of @sec-ci. It builds a two-file test suite in which one file uses `janitor`, then runs the CI test step in a fresh R process whose library holds `tinytest` and nothing else, as a runner restored from a lockfile that omits `janitor` would. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ci_run <- function(args, libs = NULL) { env <- character() if (!is.null(libs)) { empty <- file.path(tempdir(), "ci-empty-lib") dir.create(empty, showWarnings = FALSE) env <- c(paste0("R_LIBS=", libs), paste0("R_LIBS_USER=", empty), paste0("R_LIBS_SITE=", empty)) } suppressWarnings(system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript"), shQuote(c("--vanilla", args)), env = env, stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE)) } proj <- file.path(tempdir(), "ci-demo") dir.create(file.path(proj, "tests"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) writeLines("expect_equal(1 + 1, 2)", file.path(proj, "tests", "test-arith.R")) writeLines(c( "library(janitor)", "raw <- data.frame(`Patient ID` = '0001', check.names = FALSE)", "expect_equal(names(clean_names(raw)), 'patient_id')" ), file.path(proj, "tests", "test-clean.R")) ci_lib <- file.path(tempdir(), "ci-lib") dir.create(ci_lib, showWarnings = FALSE) if (!file.exists(file.path(ci_lib, "tinytest"))) { file.symlink(find.package("tinytest"), file.path(ci_lib, "tinytest")) } #> [1] TRUE red_log <- ci_run(c( "-e", sprintf("res <- tinytest::run_test_dir('%s')", file.path(proj, "tests")), "-e", "quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))" ), libs = ci_lib) cat(sprintf("%2d %s", seq_along(red_log), red_log), sep = "\n") #> 1 test-arith.R.................. 1 tests OK 21ms #> 2 Error in library(janitor) : there is no package called 'janitor' #> 3 Calls: -> lapply -> FUN -> eval -> eval -> library #> 4 Execution halted ``` ::: GitHub then appends one line of its own, `Error: Process completed with exit code 1.`, marks the step with a red cross, and skips the render step. @tbl-ci-log annotates the lines. | Line | Text begins | What it is | Act on it? | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | `test-arith.R` | A test file that ran and passed | No | | 2 | `Error in library(janitor)` | **The first error: the cause** | Yes: the package is not installed on the runner | | 3 | `Calls:` | The call stack that led to the error | Only to find which file raised it | | 4 | `Execution halted` | R stopping because of line 2 | No | | last | `Error: Process completed with exit code 1.` | GitHub's summary of the step | No; it is the same for every failure | : The red log, line by line. The line people read is the last one, and it is the only line that is identical for every failure. {#tbl-ci-log} ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Confirm that the step failed for the reason the log names, by checking the exit status and extracting the first error line: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} first_error <- grep("^Error", red_log, value = TRUE)[1] stopifnot(attr(red_log, "status") == 1, grepl("janitor", first_error), identical(first_error, red_log[2])) first_error #> [1] "Error in library(janitor) : there is no package called 'janitor'" ``` ::: On a real run, search the log for the first line that begins with `Error` (or `ERROR`, or `!` for an `rlang` error) in the failing step, and read up to three lines around it. ::: ### The fix belongs in the lockfile The cause is that `renv.lock` omits a package the code uses, so the fix is on your machine: `renv::status()` reports the package as used but not recorded, `renv::snapshot()` records it, and you commit the lockfile (@sec-renv-honest). The run turns green because the environment is now pinned, not because CI was made to tolerate it. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **Installing the missing package in the workflow makes the run green and the analysis irreproducible.** A step such as `Rscript -e 'install.packages("janitor")'` before the tests fixes the red cross in one line. The runner now has a package the lockfile does not record, at whatever version CRAN serves that day, and the green check proves exactly what it was meant to disprove: that the analysis depends on something outside `renv.lock`. Fix the lockfile, never the workflow. ::: ### Common failures | Failing step | First error looks like | Usual cause | Fix | |---|---|---|---| | `setup-renv` | A compiler or `configure` error naming a system library | A package needs a system library the runner lacks | Install it with `apt-get` in a step before `setup-renv` | | Tests | `there is no package called 'x'` | Package used but not in `renv.lock` | `renv::snapshot()` locally; commit the lockfile | | Tests | `expect_equal` failure with observed and expected values | A statistical check did not hold | Read both values; find the change that moved them | | Render | `cannot open the connection`, or `object 'x' not found` | A chunk depends on a file or object made outside the document | Build it in the pipeline, or commit the input if it is raw data | | Render | `quarto: command not found` | No Quarto setup step | Add `quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup` | : Reading a red run. {#tbl-ci-failures} The book you are reading is built this way: its workflow, `.github/workflows/render-book.yml`, restores its packages, provisions R and Python when the book needs them, and renders the whole book on every push and pull request, so that a broken chunk is caught before it reaches the published site. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} > **Context.** Below are the failing step of a GitHub Actions log, > `.github/workflows/check.yml`, and the output of > `git diff main -- renv.lock` for an R analysis compendium that > uses `renv` and `tinytest`. > > **Constraints.** Do not edit the workflow file, add an install > step, or change or skip any test. Propose changes only to > `renv.lock` (through `renv` commands) or to the analysis code. > > **Criteria.** Quote the first error line in the log and say which > step raised it. Name the cause in one sentence and give the > commands that fix it on my machine. State what `renv::status()` > and `git diff --stat` should show after the fix. *Failure mode.* The model proposes the one-line install step of the Pitfall above, or `continue-on-error: true`, because either makes the run green. *Check.* After the fix, `git diff --stat` should list `renv.lock` and nothing under `.github/` or `inst/tinytest/`, and the next run should be green. Logs are safe to send when they contain only code, package names, and test messages; a test that prints data rows puts data in the log (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A log shows `Error in library(janitor)` on line 2 and twenty more errors below it, each saying an object is not found. Which do you fix? **Answer.** Line 2. The later errors are consequences: the objects were never created because the code that would have created them needed `janitor`. Fixing them one at a time patches symptoms of a single cause, and they disappear when the package is in the lockfile. ::: ### Exercises 8. Read the log and identify the cause, why the document renders on its author's machine, and the fix. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} render_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "ci-render") dir.create(render_dir, showWarnings = FALSE) writeLines(c( "---", "title: Primary analysis", "---", "", "```{r}", "#| label: load-cohort", "cohort <- readRDS('data/derived/cohort.rds')", "```", "", "```{r}", "#| label: primary", "mean(cohort$event_30d, na.rm = TRUE)", "```" ), file.path(render_dir, "paper.qmd")) render_log <- ci_run(c("-e", sprintf(paste0( "setwd('%s'); options(cli.unicode = FALSE); ", "knitr::opts_chunk$set(error = FALSE); ", "knitr::knit('paper.qmd', quiet = TRUE)"), render_dir))) cat(render_log, sep = "\n") #> Error in `gzfile()`: #> ! cannot open the connection #> Backtrace: #> x #> 1. \-base::readRDS("data/derived/cohort.rds") #> 2. \-base::gzfile(file, "rb") #> #> Quitting from paper.qmd:5-8 [load-cohort] #> Execution halted ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} The first error, `cannot open the connection`, does not name the file; the backtrace beneath it does: `readRDS()` could not find `data/derived/cohort.rds`, in the chunk labeled `load-cohort`. The file exists on the author's machine because they built it once, by hand or with a script the document does not run, and it is a derived file, so it is (correctly) not committed. The fix is to make the pipeline build it: run the script that writes it in a step before the render, or have the document call that script, so that a clean checkout can produce it (Habit 2). Committing the `.rds` file instead would make the run green while leaving a build product that nobody can regenerate. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot(attr(render_log, "status") == 1, any(grepl("cohort.rds", render_log, fixed = TRUE))) ``` ::: ::: 9. A run fails in the `setup-renv` step. Two hundred lines into the log, the first error reads `configure: error: gdal-config not found or not executable.` What failed, and what do you change? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} A package that links to GDAL (the Geospatial Data Abstraction Library), such as `sf`, was being compiled from source, and its configure script could not find the GDAL development files on the runner. Nothing is wrong with the lockfile. Add a step before `setup-renv` that installs the system libraries, for example `sudo apt-get install -y libgdal-dev libgeos-dev libproj-dev`, or build in the project's Docker image (@sec-docker), which already has them. This is the case @sec-renv-docker describes: `renv` pins R packages, not the system libraries beneath them. ::: ## Securing the workflow {#sec-ci-security} A workflow file is code that runs with access to your repository and to any secrets you give it, and it is version-controlled and often public. Credentials, tokens, and any protected data belong in the platform's encrypted secrets, never in the workflow file; the de-identification discipline of @sec-deident applies to the pipeline as much as to the data. Three further habits come from software supply-chain security, and each is a few lines of YAML. **Pin actions by commit, not by tag.** `uses: actions/checkout@v4` names a tag, and the owner of a repository can move a tag to different code. In March 2025 the tags of the widely used `tj-actions/changed-files` action were repointed to a malicious commit that printed the secrets of the workflows using it into their run logs.[^tj-actions] A full 40-character commit SHA (secure hash algorithm identifier) cannot be moved. **Grant the workflow token the least permission that works.** Each run receives a `GITHUB_TOKEN` whose default permissions depend on repository and organization settings. A `permissions:` block at the top of the workflow sets them explicitly; a workflow that only reads code and runs checks needs `contents: read`. **Use OIDC instead of stored cloud keys.** A workflow that uploads to a cloud bucket should not hold a long-lived access key in its secrets. With OpenID Connect (OIDC), the run asks the cloud provider for short-lived credentials for one role, and the provider trusts only runs from your repository and branch. | Practice | Risk it removes | YAML | |---|---|---| | Pin by SHA | A moved tag runs code you never reviewed | `uses: owner/action@<40-hex SHA> # v4.4.0` | | Least permission | A compromised step writes to the repository | `permissions:` with `contents: read` | | OIDC | A leaked long-lived key works until someone revokes it | `id-token: write` and the provider's login action | | Dependabot | SHA pins go stale and miss security fixes | `.github/dependabot.yml`, ecosystem `github-actions` | | Secrets, never values | A token in Git history is public forever | `${{ secrets.NAME }}` | : Supply-chain basics for a workflow. {#tbl-ci-security} [^tj-actions]: The incident is CVE-2025-30066. The SHA shown for `actions/checkout` in the next listing was read from the action's repository with `git ls-remote` in October 2026. The hardened top of the workflow, with one action pinned (display-only): ```yaml permissions: contents: read jobs: check: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4.4.0 ``` The comment keeps the version readable. Pins do not update themselves, so add a Dependabot configuration that opens a pull request when a pinned action has a new release, with the SHA and the comment both updated (display-only): ```yaml # .github/dependabot.yml version: 2 updates: - package-ecosystem: github-actions directory: / schedule: interval: weekly ``` A job that needs cloud access requests the OIDC token and nothing else beyond reading the code (display-only; the role and the provider's trust policy are configured on the cloud side, and the login step is the provider's action): ```yaml permissions: contents: read id-token: write ``` ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} List every action reference in a workflow that is not pinned to a full commit SHA, and check for a `permissions:` block. The chunk writes the hardened example to a file and audits it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} audit_workflow <- function(path) { lines <- readLines(path) uses <- trimws(sub(".*uses:\\s*", "", grep("uses:", lines, value = TRUE))) uses <- sub("\\s*#.*$", "", uses) list(unpinned = uses[!grepl("@[0-9a-f]{40}$", uses)], has_permissions = any(grepl("^permissions:", lines))) } hardened <- file.path(tempdir(), "check.yml") writeLines(c( "permissions:", " contents: read", "jobs:", " check:", " runs-on: ubuntu-latest", " steps:", paste0(" - uses: actions/checkout@", "11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4.4.0") ), hardened) audit <- audit_workflow(hardened) stopifnot(length(audit$unpinned) == 0, audit$has_permissions) audit #> $unpinned #> character(0) #> #> $has_permissions #> [1] TRUE ``` ::: Run `audit_workflow()` on each file in your `.github/workflows/`; an empty `unpinned` and `TRUE` are what you want. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Your workflow pins every action to a tag such as `@v2`, the actions come from well-known organizations, and none of your secrets has leaked. Why pin by SHA anyway? **Answer.** Because a tag is a pointer its owner, or anyone who compromises the owner's account, can move, and your workflow follows it without a change to your repository. The `tj-actions` compromise reached many repositories that had never changed a line. A SHA pin means the code that runs is the code you pinned, and Dependabot turns each update into a pull request you review. ::: ### Exercises 10. If a `Dockerfile` is present it builds the project's image and renders inside it; otherwise a detection step searches `analysis/report` and provisions R when any file contains an `{r}` chunk or a `renv.lock` exists, and Python when any file contains a `{python}` chunk. The step named 'Render book (host)' or 'Render book (container)' runs `quarto render analysis/report --to html`. The deploy step, which runs only on a push to `main`, is the one that receives the Netlify secrets, and it is a third-party action: the strongest case in the file for a SHA pin. ::: ## For testthat readers {#sec-testing-testthat} `testthat` is the framework you are most likely to meet elsewhere, and where a project already depends on it, stay with it; mixing frameworks in one suite buys nothing. The discipline of this chapter is the same under either, and most of the translation is mechanical (@tbl-testing-testthat). | `tinytest` | `testthat` | |---|---| | `expect_equal(x, y, info = "...")` at the top level of the file | `test_that("...", { expect_equal(x, y) })` | | `expect_inherits(x, "tbl_df")` | `expect_s3_class(x, "tbl_df")` | | `expect_equal(names(x), c(...))` | `expect_named(x, c(...))` | | `expect_equal(sort(a), sort(b))` | `expect_setequal(a, b)` | | `expect_equal_to_reference(x, "ref.rds")`, stores the object | `expect_snapshot()`, stores printed output; `expect_snapshot_value()`, stores the value | | `tinysnapshot::expect_snapshot_plot(p, "label")` | `vdiffr::expect_doppelganger("label", p)` | | `run_test_file()`, `test_all()` | `test_file()`, `devtools::test()` | : The same tests in both frameworks. {#tbl-testing-testthat} `tinytest`'s missing functions are a choice rather than a gap: each is a plain comparison whose failure prints the two values. Visual regression testing of `ggplot2` output is the one place the two ecosystems differ in maturity. `vdiffr`, which stores an SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) file of the plot and compares later renders with it, runs only inside `testthat`; `tinysnapshot` is the `tinytest` equivalent, younger and less widely used. ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 9: test the statistics, not the shape.** Every test file needs at least one assertion against a value computed another way: by hand, in closed form, or from an independent source. A green check is only as good as what it runs: restore, test the statistics, and render; a workflow that renders without testing proves the report compiles. 2. **Habit 8: plant the bug before you trust the test, and make the quiet failure loud.** A suite you have never seen fail has not shown that it can; run one mutant per codebook rule. The exit status is the only signal CI reads; turn failed tests into a nonzero status, and never set `continue-on-error` on a check. 3. **Habit 4: pin the environment, including the CI's own.** Run the tests in CI on every push, restore from the lockfile, pin actions by SHA, and fix a red restore in `renv.lock`, never with an install step in the workflow. ## Cumulative practice 11. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-teams).* Review a colleague's test suite rather than their code. For each test, decide whether it checks statistical content or only structure, and find at least one test that would pass even if the function under test were subtly wrong. Write the mutant that survives, propose the value-level assertion that kills it, and deliver the review as a pull-request comment. 12. *Cumulative (uses @sec-renv).* Write the complete workflow for the HF-HOME compendium: it runs on pull requests and on pushes to `main`, sets `contents: read`, restores `renv.lock`, installs Quarto, fails on any failed `tinytest` test, and renders `analysis/report`. Add the Dependabot file, and check both against @tbl-ci-checklist and @tbl-ci-security. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} 12. The workflow: ```yaml # .github/workflows/check.yml name: Check analysis on: push: branches: [main] pull_request: permissions: contents: read jobs: check: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@ # v4.4.0 - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@ # v2 with: use-public-rspm: true - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@ # v2 - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@ # v2 - name: Run tests run: | Rscript -e 'res <- tinytest::test_all()' \ -e 'quit(status = as.integer(tinytest::any_fail(res)))' - name: Render report run: quarto render analysis/report ``` Replace each `` with the commit the tag points to, from `git ls-remote https://github.com// refs/tags/`; for a tag that `git ls-remote` lists twice, use the line ending in `^{}`, which is the commit. The Dependabot file is the one in @sec-ci-security. Against the checklist: restore, test, and render are each a step that fails the job, no secret appears, the token can only read, and every action is pinned. The workflow needs no secrets at all, which is the best case. ::: 13. *On your own work (no key).* Add unit tests for two functions from an analysis of yours (a typical case, an edge case, and an error), an integration test on a synthetic fixture that exercises every branch, and a CI workflow that runs them; push it and confirm the run is green. Even a one-off analysis benefits from tests: they catch regressions when you refactor mid-analysis, they serve as executable documentation of expected behavior, and they detect silent failures when upstream data change format. The cost of writing a handful of tests is small; the cost of silently mis-analyzing data is much larger. 2. A unit test exercises a single function with known inputs and checks the output. An integration test runs a pipeline segment (multiple functions) on synthetic data and checks the pipeline's output. An end-to-end test runs the full analysis pipeline from raw data to final figures and tables. Unit tests are fast and narrow; end-to-end tests are slow and broad; integration tests sit in between, with good cost-benefit for analytic pipelines. 3. Continuous integration automatically builds and checks a project on every change: it reconstructs the environment, runs the tests, and renders the report. It automates the clean-state rerun that a disciplined analyst might do by hand occasionally, but does it on every push and on a machine that is not theirs. 'It renders on my machine' depends on packages, files, and manual steps that exist only on your machine and may not be recorded. CI reconstructs the analysis from the committed sources and `renv.lock` on a clean machine, so a passing run demonstrates that the analysis is reproducible from what is actually in the repository, not from the state of your laptop.
